name: Ketamine
summary: A drug where the route changes not just the speed but the substance. Swallowed, over 80% of a ketamine dose is converted by the liver into norketamine before it ever reaches the brain — and norketamine is a different, longer, more sedating drug. Oral ketamine is substantially a norketamine experience.
mechanism: Blocks the NMDA glutamate receptor channel from the inside, which it can only do when the channel is already open — so it preferentially silences the most active circuits. The dissociative effect comes from functionally disconnecting cortical regions rather than depressing them. Its rapid antidepressant effect is thought to involve a downstream burst of synaptic plasticity, not the block itself.

two_compartment.note: Fat-soluble and rapidly redistributed, so a single dose wears off by moving into tissue well before it is eliminated.

insufflated.note: The common recreational route. Partly absorbed nasally and partly swallowed, so it produces both a ketamine peak and a delayed norketamine tail.

iv.note: Anaesthetic and clinical antidepressant route. Entirely parent drug, with no first-pass conversion at all.

im.note: Nearly complete absorption with a smooth rise; the usual route for veterinary and field anaesthesia.

oral.note: Only about a sixth survives the liver, and what emerges is mostly norketamine. The result is longer, heavier and less lucid than the same amount by any other route — not a weaker version of the same thing.

pathways.name: Norketamine
pathways.note: Active, roughly a third as potent, and longer-lived than the parent at around 5 hours. After an oral dose it is the dominant species.

pathways.name: Hydroxynorketamines
pathways.note: Of research interest for the antidepressant effect, which may not require NMDA blockade at all.

risk: Redosing is the main acute problem: the effect fades by redistribution in 20-45 minutes while most of the drug is still in the body, so repeated doses stack into a far deeper state than intended.
Loss of airway reflexes plus vomiting is the usual mechanism of harm; ketamine rarely stops breathing on its own, but someone unconscious on their back is in danger regardless of the drug.

Ketamine-induced uropathy is the distinctive chronic harm of heavy regular use — a painful, sometimes irreversible contracted bladder. It is dose and frequency related and is the reason frequent use is far riskier than occasional use.
With other depressants, particularly alcohol and benzodiazepines, the combined sedation and vomiting risk is much greater. See interactions.
